name: ilovemd
tagline: Browser-based Markdown workspace: write, preview, and convert Markdown to and from other document formats.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: Markdown tooling is the most solved problem in software: the parsers, the renderers, the syntax highlighters, and the PDF exporters are all mature open source libraries that an agent can wire together in an afternoon. A local editor with live preview, file open and save, and HTML plus PDF export is a genuinely one-session build with no third-party dependency. The hard parts, if you want them, are the conversion edge cases: DOCX in, tables that survive the round trip, footnotes, embedded images. Pandoc handles most of that and it is one shell call away. What you are actually paying a hosted tool for is not having to install anything and having it work on a borrowed laptop.
coreLoopDIY: A local web app that edits Markdown with live preview, opens and saves .md files from disk, and exports clean HTML and PDF.
requirements: optional: pandoc installed locally if you want DOCX and other format conversion
whatYouLose: Zero-install access from any machine, which is the actual product
Battle-tested conversion for messy real-world DOCX and PDF inputs
Whatever collaboration, sharing links, or cloud sync the hosted version offers
Mobile usability, since your build will be a desktop browser tool
Someone else maintaining the export pipeline when a library changes its API
moatNotes: The moat here is convenience and trust that the file you paste in does not go somewhere weird, not technology.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because Markdown conversion is the kind of task that shows up once a month, unpredictably, often on a machine that is not yours. Nobody wants to npm install a personal editor to turn one README into a PDF before a meeting. A hosted tool that loads in two seconds and handles the ugly DOCX your client sent is worth a small recurring fee to the people who hit that problem regularly, even though the underlying code is trivially reproducible.
notes: If your Markdown needs are personal and repeatable, this is a folder of scripts, not a subscription.
prompt:
Build a local-first Markdown workspace as a single web app. Empty folder, no accounts, no cloud, no telemetry.

Stack, no substitutions:
- Vite + React + TypeScript
- CodeMirror 6 for the editor pane, with Markdown mode
- markdown-it for rendering, plus plugins for tables, footnotes, and task lists
- highlight.js for fenced code blocks
- Tailwind for styling, keep it plain and dense
- A tiny Node/Express sidecar (same repo, `npm run dev` starts both) for filesystem access and export

Core features, all required:
1. Split view: editor left, live rendered preview right, scroll-synced. Toggle to editor-only or preview-only.
2. Open a .md file from disk and save back to the same path. Also "save as". Use the Express sidecar, not the File System Access API, so it works in any browser.
3. Autosave the current buffer to a local `.workspace/` folder so a crash never loses text.
4. Export the current document to standalone HTML (inlined CSS, no external assets) and to PDF (render the HTML in headless Chromium via Puppeteer in the sidecar).
5. Paste or drag an image into the editor: write it into an `assets/` folder next to the .md file and insert a relative Markdown image link.
6. A word count, character count, and reading time in a status bar.
7. Keyboard shortcuts: bold, italic, link, code block, heading cycle, save.

Optional, behind a feature check:
- If `pandoc` is on PATH, expose "import DOCX" and "export DOCX" endpoints that shell out to it. If it is not installed, hide those buttons and say why. Do not bundle or vendor pandoc.

Out of scope, do not build: user accounts, sharing links, sync, collaborative editing, Mermaid or LaTeX rendering, a mobile layout, a plugin system.

Any config goes in .env with a committed .env.example. Ship a README with exact run instructions and a one-paragraph note on what the pandoc path does and does not handle.
